Source: Facebook

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — A final farewell to American Samoa Meteorologist Leilua Mase Akapo, longtime American Samoa meteorologist, a post he held for decades until his retirement.

Leilua was the face of every major natural disaster including some of the most memorable Hurricane Ofa, Tusi and Val to tropical cyclones, floods and the devastating earthquake and tsunami of 2009.

We all tuned in as he kept the public informed.

He was both the trust and the calm of American Samoa during such times. Manuia lau malaga Mr. Akapo Akapo, as he was known to many of us.

Heartfelt condolences to his children and family from the local community and Samoa News.

Governor to launch anti-drug awareness campaign as public concerns grow over widespread drug abuse

2026-10-27

The problem can no longer be ignored, says territory’s leaders

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA— The launch of Governor Pulaali'i Nikolao Pula's planned anti-drug awareness campaign next month comes at a critical time for American Samoa, as growing concerns mount over the spread of illegal drugs throughout the Territory.

Over the past several years, community leaders, law enforcement officials, educators, church representatives, and families have increasingly voiced alarm over the widespread presence of crystal methamphetamine, commonly known as ice. Once considered a problem affecting only a limited segment of the population, drug abuse is now viewed as a crisis reaching into nearly every part of society.

Officials say the problem no longer affects only adults. Reports and community observations indicate that drug use is impacting people across multiple age groups, from middle-aged adults and young people, including high school students, to, in some cases, children of elementary school age.

The growing reach of the drug has heightened concerns about its devastating effects on families, public safety, education, and the overall wellbeing of communities throughout the Territory.

Against this backdrop, Governor Pulaali'i's planned campaign is expected to place renewed public attention on the dangers of substance abuse while encouraging a united response involving government agencies, churches, families, schools, villages, and community organizations. Many believe the drug problem has reached an alarming level and requires a coordinated effort from every sector of society.

The issue came under the spotlight during the final Senate Standing Committee hearing of the 39th Legislature before lawmakers adjourned for their end-of-year recess. Members of the Senate Public Safety and Homeland Security Committee summoned officials from the Department of Public Safety (DPS), the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and Customs to explain their ongoing efforts to combat illegal drugs and strengthen border enforcement.

Chief Customs Officer Iuliano Falaniko told senators that Customs personnel detain individuals caught attempting to smuggle drugs through the Territory's ports of entry and immediately refer the cases to Homeland Security investigators. The same procedure applies to individuals who go to the Fagatogo Post Office to collect packages or parcels from off-island that are found to contain concealed narcotics.

Falaniko explained that in previous years such cases were referred directly to the DPS, which would then assume responsibility for detaining suspects and conducting investigations. However, a change in the law has shifted primary responsibility for handling these cases to the DHS.

"The process begins with a referral to the Attorney General," DHS Director Vaeotagaloa Glenn Lefiti explained. "Our responsibility is to conduct the investigation and provide a complete report of our findings. The Attorney General's Office reviews the facts, evaluates the evidence, and determines whether criminal charges are warranted."

The change became official after legislation approved by the Fono last year granted DHS authority to arrest and detain travelers attempting to bring illegal drugs into American Samoa through ports of entry, as well as individuals seeking to claim drug-laden packages arriving from off-island. Under the law, these investigations now fall under the jurisdiction of DHS.

Lefiti emphasized that while Homeland Security has been assigned responsibility for border interdiction and related investigations, DPS continues to focus on local drug enforcement operations within communities. He stressed that both agencies work closely together, along with Customs officials, in identifying, investigating, and apprehending offenders.

The DHS Director also highlighted the department's partnerships with federal agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), in efforts to protect American Samoa's borders from drug smuggling operations, human trafficking, and other transnational criminal activities.

Several senators, however, expressed concern about what they viewed as overlapping responsibilities between DHS and DPS.

Senator Togiola T.A. Tulafono argued that the apparent duplication of duties could be undermining the effectiveness of anti-drug enforcement efforts. He pointed to figures contained in a report submitted by Lefiti indicating that only five drug-related cases had been recorded during 2025.

According to Togiola, that number appeared inconsistent with the numerous arrests reported by DPS during a series of drug raids, as well as the quantities of methamphetamine seized in those operations.

"This doesn't add up," Togiola remarked, questioning whether different agencies were using separate reporting systems that failed to present a complete picture of the Territory's drug problem.

Another issue raised by senators was the growing threat of fentanyl, a highly potent synthetic opioid that has fueled a deadly overdose crisis in many parts of the United States.

At the close of the hearing, Senate President Tuaolo Manaia Fruean asked whether Homeland Security, Public Safety, and Customs were adequately prepared to prevent fentanyl from entering American Samoa and to respond should it gain a foothold in the Territory.

Lefiti's response was blunt.

"No," the Homeland Security Director admitted.

He told lawmakers that American Samoa currently lacks the resources, specialized equipment, and training necessary to effectively address the unique dangers posed by fentanyl. He said DHS is actively pursuing federal grant funding to strengthen detection capabilities and provide advanced training for personnel.

The concerns raised at the hearing highlight the urgency behind Governor Pulaali'i's upcoming anti-drug awareness campaign.

Speaking at a recent press conference, the Governor stressed that defeating the Territory's drug problem will require more than law enforcement efforts alone. He called on families, churches, schools, village leaders, and community organizations to become active partners in the fight against illegal drugs.

He warned that the growing drug epidemic is tearing families apart, contributing to crime, and placing the future of many young people at risk.

"This has become a very serious problem," Pulaali'i said. "We must come together as a community to address it before more lives are lost and more families are harmed."

The campaign, which is scheduled to begin in early November, will be spearheaded by the newly established eight-member Opioid and Substance Abuse Council (OSAC) operating under the Governor's Drug Control Office.

The council has been tasked with coordinating public education campaigns, prevention initiatives, and substance abuse programs throughout the Territory. It will also serve as the government's primary advisory and oversight body for opioid-related and substance abuse initiatives, ensuring compliance with the Opioid Settlement Agreement and its approved abatement strategies.

Members of the council include Assistant Attorney General Louise Lafitaga, Acting Commissioner of Public Safety Lauti Tautalasoo Moliga, Department of Health psychiatrist Dr. Peni Biukoto, Homeland Security Director Vaeotagaloa Glenn Lefiti, Deputy Treasurer Levi Reese, clinical psychologist Dr. Jueta Eta McCutchan, faith-based community advocate Rev. Iasepi Ulu, and victims advocate Ipu Lefiti of the Pae ma le Auli Organization.

The Governor emphasized that while government agencies have a responsibility to enforce the law and provide resources, lasting success will depend on the willingness of the entire community to become involved.

"The government cannot address this alone," he said. "Our families, churches, schools, and villages all have a role in protecting our people and helping prevent drug use in our communities."

As American Samoa prepares for the launch of the campaign, many hope it will mark the beginning of a broader Territory-wide effort to confront a problem that residents, church leaders, lawmakers, and law enforcement officials alike say can no longer be ignored.

BACGROUND

In the meantime, the territory is currently awaiting a new facility that is being built for the comprehensive care for individuals receiving behavioral health, mental health, and substance abuse rehabilitation services — the American Samoa Department of Health’s new Behavioral Health & Drug and Alcohol Rehabilitation Clinic.

The governor has commended the collaborative efforts of the Department of Health, the ARPA Oversight Office, and all partners involved in moving this project forward. The facility is being built by Silva Group Corporation.

Completion of new Airport Terminal parking lot expansion targeted for June 2027

2026-10-26

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMMOA — The Port Administration of American Samoa (PAAS) has provided an update on the development of the Airport Terminal Parking Lot Expansion Project at the Pago Pago International Airport (PPG). The critical infrastructure project is moving forward steadily with overall completion of 35%, and target completion date of June 30, 2027, according to the media release.

PAAS Director Barney Sene said, “The Airport Terminal Parking Lot Expansion Project represents an important investment in the future of the Pago Pago International Airport and the infrastructure needed to support the new Airport Terminal Facility construction. Although much of the current work is taking place underground and may not be readily visible to the public, these improvements to the drainage, sanitary, power, and utility systems are essential components of the overall new airport terminal project. We are pleased with the progress being made and appreciate the continued efforts of our contractor and utility partners.”

The Director added, “We understand that construction activities can create temporary challenges for our airport users and the community. We greatly appreciate the patience, cooperation, and understanding of our travelers, visitors, and residents as this important work continues. Our priority remains completing the project safely and efficiently while maintaining continuous airport operations.”

Contractor Paramount Builders, Inc. has maintained an active pace of work despite recent rainy weather. Construction activities are currently focused on vital underground drainage and utility infrastructure to support the future new Airport Terminal Facility. Recent progress includes:

Construction activities are currently focused on underground drainage and utility infrastructure to support the future new Airport Terminal Facility. [Photo: PIOA/ Woolpert]

DRAINAGE AND STRUCTURES:

Completion of cast-in-place concrete culverts, structure base pours, and formwork, including the pouring of storm structures and protective concrete covers.

SANITARY SUSTEMS:

Successful installation of 160 linear feet of 12-inch sanitary piping on the north side of the site, alongside necessary density testing.

UTILITY MODERNAZATION:

Close coordination with local utility providers to manage underground power connections, safely navigate junction box placements, and install utility poles to support temporary telecommunications cables to the airport terminal.

To maintain an active and safe construction zone while ensuring continuous airport operations, a public traffic setup has been established at the main parking lot entrance and exit. This requires a temporary road rerouting, complete with specialized striping patterns, directional signs, and safety barricades.

PAAS acknowledges that navigating construction zones can be challenging and extends its formal appreciation to the public, airport travelers, visitors, and the wider community for their continued patience, cooperation, and understanding as we build a more modern, secure, and optimal facility to serve American Samoa.

The Terminal Parking Lot Expansion Project is an important step toward providing a more modern, secure, efficient, and functional airport facility to better serve the people of American Samoa and visitors to the territory.

Samoa's forgotten fagufagu makes a comeback

2026-10-26

Source: Samoa Observer

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — A traditional Samoan musical instrument that disappeared from the country's soundscape more than a century ago is making a comeback, with efforts underway to restore the knowledge of how it was made and played.

The fagufagu, or nose flute in English, once used in traditional music, poetry and ceremonial practices, is being reintroduced through workshops and performances involving Samoan and other Pacific practitioners.

Tanuvasa Tau’ili’ili Alpha Maiava, co-director of Talanoa Arts Forum, is among those

According to Tanuvasa, the fagufagu began disappearing from Samoa's traditional soundscape during the 1800s, with Christianity, colonisation and Western musical influences contributing to its decline.

Over time, the knowledge of how to construct and play the instrument was also lost as fewer people passed these skills on.

With limited documentation available in Samoa, those involved in the revival have turned to other Pacific countries where similar traditions have survived.

Tanuvasa has worked with Tongan master instrumentalist Tu’ifonualava Kaivelata and the Hikule’ao o Ono’aho collective, known in Samoan as Si’uleo o Anamua.

Tongan practitioner Saia Tuitahi also visited Samoa to demonstrate construction techniques to Galumalemana Steven Percival at the Tiapapata Arts Centre.

In February 2026, workshops were held at five locations across Samoa as part of the Samoa Arts Fono, introducing participants to the fagufagu and other traditional sound practices.

Tanuvasa said the instrument was beginning to appear more frequently in performances, although much of its traditional knowledge remained to be recovered.

“While the instrument is now appearing more frequently in performances, much of the deeper knowledge surrounding its construction, cultivation, and traditional use is only now beginning to be reclaimed,” he said.

The revival aims to ensure future generations can not only play the fagufagu but also understand its place in Samoan culture.

Former intern in Amata’s local office talks about her time as a Peace Corps Volunteer

2026-10-23

Source: Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata’s D.C. staff

Washington, D.C. — Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata is congratulating Peace Corps Volunteer Rosalina Macon, a former intern in the congressional office, and currently featured in an article on the Peace Corps website. She is from Manu’a and the villages of Utumea, Fagaalu, and Vailoa.

In her studies at North Carolina A&T State University, Rosalina twice had the opportunity to study abroad. Those in turn inspired her desire to reconnect deeply with her Samoan heritage, increase fluency in the Samoan language, and consider the Peace Corps with the idea of possibly serving in Samoa. Instead, she was offered the opportunity for a new experience staying in the Indo-Pacific region and serving in Indonesia, the world’s largest archipelagic nation of islands. It is the world’s fourth-most populous country, and in the top 15 in the world by total land area.

In Indonesia, after three months of focused training, then moving there on her birthday, she began teaching English while working on her use of the local language, Sundanese. She quickly established friendships and a special support network with three local English teachers she now calls her “sisters,” as well as finding a welcoming community from the locals.

Along with her teaching assignment at Islamic Middle School in Java, the world’s most populous island, she and the teachers there are implementing fun vocabulary words, strengthening students’ opportunities through an English club outside the structure of the classroom, and planning for an English camp.

Rosalina said, “It has been a privilege to serve as a Peace Corps volunteer in Indonesia. I’ve been blessed to work alongside my Indonesian counterparts and community to create projects together, and along the way I’ve learned so much about Indonesian culture while getting to share my own in return. Not every day is easy, but I’m constantly reminded that I represent more than myself. I carry my family and my communities in American Samoa and South Carolina with me, and I’m proud to represent them. Though service isn’t a foreign concept to me, this experience has simply been a continuation of that lifelong commitment.”

“Congratulations to Rosalina, who worked as an intern in our office in Tutuila. She has a bright future through her intelligence, assertiveness, and deep interest in influencing policy for the betterment of people’s lives,” said Congresswoman Amata. “She’s putting those interests to great use right now with the Peace Corps, which will lead to more open doors. I know her family and friends in American Samoa and South Carolina are following this phase of her life closely, and we are proud of her in American Samoa!”

Congresswoman Amata serves as Co-Chairman of the bipartisan Peace Corps Caucus in the U.S. House of Representatives, with Congressman John Garamendi (D-CA). They have worked for reauthorization legislation and emphasized the expansion of the Peace Corps back into more nations following pandemic recovery, including the Indo-Pacific region.

ASTCA top officials clarify A250 expense-share and COO compensation issues

2026-10-22

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The Senate Government Operations Investigative Committee continued its inquiry into the American Samoa Telecommunications Authority (ASTCA) on Monday, focusing on expenditures related to the America250 (A250) celebrations and questions surrounding the employment contracts of former Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Chuck Leota, who now serves as the authority's Chief Operations Officer (COO).

Appearing before the committee were ASTCA CEO Folasaitu Sorepa Thomas and COO Chuck Leota, who were called to provide testimony and clarify issues that have been the subject of previous hearings.

Before taking testimony, Committee Chairman Senator Togiola T.A. Tulafono outlined the matters senators hoped to address during the hearing.

Regarding the A250 celebrations, Togiola said lawmakers were seeking a detailed accounting of the funds spent by ASTCA in support of the event. He asked whether a final financial report had been prepared showing the total amount expended and providing a complete breakdown of all costs incurred.

The senator explained that it was the committee's understanding that the A250 celebration was co-sponsored by ASTCA and the Reid Group, with both parties reportedly agreeing to share the overall cost of the event.

However, Togiola noted that documents provided to the committee did not show any reimbursement or payment from the Reid Group for its alleged share of the expenses.

"Our understanding is that ASTCA and the Reid Group agreed to split the costs," Togiola said. "However, the report provided to this committee does not indicate that ASTCA received any payment from the Reid Group toward those expenses."

Lawmakers indicated they wanted to determine the total cost of the event, each party's financial obligations, and whether ASTCA ultimately absorbed expenses that should have been shared.

The committee then turned its attention to issues surrounding Leota's employment contracts with ASTCA and the controversial child support payment that was reportedly made using ASTCA funds, a matter that has generated significant public scrutiny.

Togiola requested copies of Leota's original employment agreement signed during the Lemanu-Talauega Administration, when he was appointed Chief Executive Officer, as well as the contract later executed under the current Pula-Pulu Administration for his position as Chief Operations Officer (CEO).

The senator said the committee continues to seek clarification regarding ASTCA's reported obligation to compensate Leota in the amount of approximately $135,000 following the termination of his original CEO contract.

"The committee wants clarification on the circumstances that, in your belief, have resulted in ASG being obligated to pay him the significant amount of $135,000 because of the alleged violation of the terms of the original contract," Togiola stated.

"We want a clear explanation of the terms of these contracts and what exactly were the terms that were allegedly violated, which has placed ASG in debt to Mr. Leota."

According to Togiola, previous testimony by CEO Folasaitu indicated that Leota's original contract was a three-year agreement that should have extended into the current administration.

However, senators were informed that the contract was terminated after the change in administration.

"It seems to us that this termination has led you to believe that ASG became obligated to compensate Mr. Leota," Togiola said.

The senator pointed out that testimony from prior hearings showed Leota subsequently entered into a new contract with ASTCA as Chief Operations Officer (COO) and continued receiving the same annual salary of $135,000, along with the same benefits provided under his CEO contract.

"If our records of previous testimony are accurate," Togiola continued, "what exactly caused ASG to become liable for compensation when he did not appear to suffer any financial damages?"

He noted that while the CEO contract may have been terminated before its expiration date, Leota was immediately retained in another executive position at the same salary level.

"The original contract may have been prematurely terminated, but the second contract for the COO position provided the same salary and benefits that he was already entitled to under the original agreement," the senator observed.

Togiola also sought clarification regarding the circumstances surrounding the termination itself.

He questioned whether the decision was reached through mutual agreement between Leota and ASTCA, whether Leota objected to the termination, or whether the action was taken unilaterally by the authority or administration.

"And the final question is, was the termination of Mr. Leota's original contract done after an agreement was reached between him and ASG?" Togiola asked. "Or was it done despite his objections? Whose decision was it, and how did that result in ASG becoming obligated to pay compensation of $135,000?"

The committee chairman stated that, based on the information currently available to senators, lawmakers remain unconvinced that the circumstances justify compensation to Leota.

Togiola said the committee's preliminary view is that ASTCA and the government should not have been required to make such a payment if Leota suffered no measurable financial loss as a result of the transition from CEO to COO.

AMERICA250

Responding to questions from Committee Chairman Senator Togiola regarding the financial contributions of the Reid Group as a co-sponsor of the America250 celebration, current ASTCA CEO Folasaitu provided what she said was a detailed accounting of the event's expenses and the payments received from the private-sector partner.

According to Folasaitu, the total cost of the America250 celebration amounted to $688,133.52. Under the co-sponsorship arrangement, the expenses were divided equally between the American Samoa Telecommunications Authority (ASTCA) and the Reid Group, resulting in each party's share totaling $344,066.76.

Addressing concerns raised by senators that committee records did not reflect any contribution from the Reid Group, Folasaitu testified that payments had in fact been received and properly documented.

She told lawmakers that ASTCA received two wire transfers totaling $288,000 from the Reid Group through Ford Samoa Motors on July 18, 2026. In addition, ASTCA received another payment of $128,915 on August 26, 2026.

Folasaitu further explained that, beyond the funds deposited directly into ASTCA's account, the Reid Group also paid invoices totaling approximately $55,000 related to the event. Those payments, she said, were made directly and therefore did not appear as deposits in ASTCA's financial records.

According to the CEO, all transactions are reflected in ASTCA's bank statements and supporting financial documentation. She informed the committee that copies of the wire transfers, bank records, invoices, and other supporting documents had been compiled and submitted to senators for review.

In addition, Folasaitu stated that copies of the co-sponsorship agreement with the Reid Group had been submitted. All bills have been settled and the A250 organizing committee has been dissolved after all records were reconciled.

Senator Togiola T.A. Tulafono questioned why key information in the financial documents submitted to the committee had been redacted, specifically noting that certain account numbers had been blacked out.

In response, the ASTCA CEO said the authority would resubmit the documents with the redacted information restored.

Togiola further observed that large portions of the report had been redacted, with the exception of entries identifying Samoa Motors. He questioned why some information had been withheld from lawmakers conducting the investigation.

Folasaitu explained that the documents contained personal and confidential information relating to ASTCA customers. According to the CEO, some transactions reflected customer credits and account activity that could reveal private financial information when payments exceeded amounts reflected in bank statements.

She told senators that ASTCA had redacted the information to protect customer privacy, not to conceal details related to the committee's inquiry.

However, Folasaitu assured lawmakers that if the committee required access to the complete records, ASTCA would provide the information after consulting with its legal counsel to ensure that customer confidentiality requirements were properly addressed.

The CEO also clarified that the bank statements submitted to the committee were from ASTCA's account at the Territorial Bank of American Samoa (TBAS), which she described as the authority's primary banking institution.

Folasaitu noted that ASTCA maintains only one other banking relationship, that with Syniverse Bank, which is used exclusively for telecommunications roaming services. She explained that the arrangement is a Federal Communications Commission (FCC) requirement and is standard practice among telecommunications providers.

Folasaitu also clarified that the report previously submitted to the committee was essentially the same report lawmakers already had in their possession, with the only differences being the additional supporting documents and financial information she had provided during the latest hearing.

She explained that the supplemental documents, including bank records, wire-transfer confirmations, and invoices, were submitted to address questions raised by committee members regarding the A250 celebration expenses and the Reid Group's financial contributions.

ASTCA COO CHUCK LEOTA

The committee then shifted its focus to matters surrounding former ASTCA CEO Chuck Leota's employment contracts.

Senate President Tuaolo Manaia Fruean requested a detailed explanation of Leota's contractual arrangements with ASTCA, including the transition from his position as CEO under the previous administration to his current role as COO.

In response, ASTCA CEO Folasaitu explained that by the time she assumed leadership of the authority, the negotiations concerning Leota's employment had already been completed, with the terms of Leota's contract negotiated and agreed upon by the ASTCA Board of Directors and the Governor, before she became CEO.

She indicated that she was therefore not directly involved in the discussions that led to either the termination of Leota's original CEO contract or the subsequent agreement that placed him in the position of COO.

Folasaitu testified that some members of the ASTCA Board were already aware of the circumstances surrounding the termination of Chuck Leota's contract as CEO before the matter was brought to her attention.

According to CEO Folasaitu, after learning of the situation she continued to work with Leota and, at one point, appointed him to represent ASTCA at a telecommunications meeting in Fiji. However, those plans were later disrupted when Leota was unable to travel because he could not use a Certificate of Identity (CI) for the trip.

Folasaitu told senators that she subsequently raised questions about Leota's employment status and contract during a meeting of the ASTCA Board. At the time, she said, she was not informed that board members had already discussed the issue and had supported the decision to terminate his CEO contract.

She testified that her understanding of the Board's role evolved later during legislative hearings when then-ASTCA Board Chairman Avamua Dave Haleck testified before the Fono. According to Folasaitu, Haleck stated that he had met with Governor Pulaali'i Nikolao Pula, and that it was ultimately the Governor who decided that Leota's CEO contract should be terminated.

However, Folasaitu said subsequent developments revealed that the Board had also played a role in the matter.

She pointed out that the Board's involvement became evident through the settlement agreement that was later reached and supported by the Board, indicating that board members had participated in discussions relating to Leota's contract and the resolution of any claims arising from its termination.

Folasaitu also shared her personal views regarding the decision to remove Chuck Leota from the position of Chief Executive Officer, telling senators that she did not believe the termination should have occurred.

"If you were to ask me then whether terminating Chuck Leota's contract as CEO was the right thing to do, I would have said they should have never removed Chuck," Folasaitu testified.

She explained that her concerns stemmed from provisions of the executive order governing ASTCA's management structure and the respective authority of the Board of Directors and the CEO.

According to Folasaitu, the executive order gives the ASTCA Board the authority to hire the Chief Executive Officer, while the responsibility for hiring other personnel rests with the CEO.

"The reason is that it does not align with the executive order," she stated. "The Board is responsible for hiring the CEO, but the hiring of all other staff is the sole responsibility of the CEO."

In her view, if the administration or the Board wished to make leadership changes, they should have allowed Leota to remain in place until a successor was selected or appointed him to serve in an acting capacity while they determined the authority's future direction.

"They should have waited until a new CEO was selected or kept him as Acting CEO until they figured out exactly what they wanted to do," Folasaitu said.

She further explained that the arrangement ultimately reached with Leota involved removing him from the CEO position and appointing him instead as COO. In exchange, she said, Leota agreed to forego severance benefits that might otherwise have been available under his original contract.

However, Folasaitu told senators that even the negotiated settlement raised questions about compliance with the authority's governing rules.

She argued that the arrangement still did not fully conform to the provisions of a 2018 executive order that clearly defines the duties and responsibilities of the ASTCA Board and the CEO, including who has authority over employment decisions within the organization.

According to Folasaitu, the executive order establishes a framework intended to separate policymaking and oversight responsibilities from day-to-day management functions. As a result, she suggested that the handling of Leota's transition from CEO to COO may not have been entirely consistent with those requirements.

Folasaitu further testified that she amended Leota's contract because, in her view, ASTCA remained obligated to pay the severance benefits provided under his original employment agreement.

Folasaitu also informed the committee that, as part of the restructuring of Leota's employment arrangement, she removed him from career service status and placed him on a contractual agreement as COO.

She explained that the change was made during the process of negotiating a resolution to issues arising from the termination of Leota's original CEO contract. Under the new arrangement, Leota no longer served as a career service employee but instead held the COO position under the terms of a separate employment contract.

According to Folasaitu, the revised agreement was intended to address concerns surrounding the termination of the CEO contract while allowing ASTCA to retain Leota's experience and institutional knowledge in a senior management role.

According to the CEO, the basis for that position is documented in communications and transcripts involving discussions with the Chief Justice regarding the contractual dispute and proposed settlement.

The hearing then turned to the controversial issue of ASTCA's payment of a child-support obligation on Leota's behalf, a matter that has been the subject of public criticism and previous legislative scrutiny.

Senate President Tuaolo questioned why ASTCA became directly involved in making the payment rather than simply paying Leota any compensation or severance to which he may have been entitled under the settlement agreement.

"Why didn't you just give Leota his severance pay instead of going to all that trouble of carrying out what he should have done himself as he is obligated by law to do?" Tuaolo asked.

In response, Folasaitu defended the decision, arguing that the arrangement was intended to ensure transparency and accountability in the use of ASTCA funds.

She explained that directing the payment to its intended recipient removed any uncertainty about how the money would be used and ensured that the obligation was satisfied in full.

According to Folasaitu, had the funds been paid directly to Leota as a lump-sum settlement, questions could have arisen over whether the money was ultimately used for its intended purpose.

"It was done for transparency and accountability," Folasaitu stated. "If the funds had simply been given to Mr. Leota, there could have been speculation about whether the money was actually used to satisfy the child-support obligation or spent on something else."

She told senators that the decision was made to ensure the payment went directly toward the obligation in question rather than passing through a third party first.

Senator Olo Uluao Letuli later questioned ASTCA COO Leota about the status of his child-support obligation, noting that the approximately $110,000 paid by ASTCA was less than the $135,000 amount that had reportedly been ordered by the court.

Olo asked whether the matter had been fully resolved, given the apparent difference between the amount paid and the amount originally sought.

In response, Leota testified that the issue had been settled locally. However, he explained that proceedings related to the matter were still continuing in the mainland courts and remained under negotiation.

According to Leota, while the local aspects of the child-support case had been resolved, discussions involving the mainland court system had not yet been fully concluded.

Senator Olo indicated that he viewed the child-support issue as a private matter and a legal obligation that Leota was personally responsible for fulfilling. While expressing reservations about delving further into the issue, Olo said his primary concern was understanding the circumstances surrounding Leota's employment arrangement with ASTCA.

The senator asked Leota whether there had been a verbal agreement, written agreement, executive order, or any other understanding under which he was offered the position of COO in exchange for waiving or foregoing severance benefits tied to the termination of his CEO contract.

In response, Leota recounted the events that occurred following the change in administration.

Leota testified that shortly after the Pula and Pulu Administration took office, he was summoned to meet with Governor Pulaali'i. According to Leota, the two held a lengthy discussion during which the Governor explained that the new administration intended to implement leadership changes throughout government departments, agencies, and public authorities.

Leota said the Governor informed him that the decision was not personal but was part of a broader effort to fulfill promises made during the campaign.

According to Leota, Governor Pulaali'i acknowledged his years of service to ASTCA and thanked him for his contributions to the authority.

Leota testified that the Governor then asked him to remain at ASTCA and assist the new chief executive officer who would eventually be appointed to lead the telecommunications authority.

He told senators that he appreciated the Governor's recognition of his service and welcomed the opportunity to continue contributing to the organization he had worked hard to improve over the years. Leota said he accepted the Governor's request and agreed to remain with ASTCA to help ensure a smooth transition of leadership.

Leota further testified that, following his discussion with Governor Pulaali'i, he requested to be transferred from his contractual position as CEO to a career service position and, in return, agreed to forgo any severance benefits that may have been available under his original contract.

According to Leota, the request was approved, and he served as a career service employee at ASTCA from May 2025 through January 2026.

He explained that the situation later changed when he was selected to attend a telecommunications meeting in Fiji but was unable to travel using a CI. After informing CEO Folasaitu of the problem, the two discussed the possibility of changing his employment status again.

Leota told senators that those discussions eventually led to the renegotiation of his employment arrangement, resulting in his appointment as COO under a contractual agreement.

However, he emphasized that his earlier decision to move into career service status should not be viewed as a trade-off or exchange for other benefits.

According to Leota, the transfer was made in good faith to accommodate the transition to the new administration and to allow him to continue serving ASTCA in a different capacity.

Leota also disputed claims that he continued receiving the same salary he earned as CEO after moving into the COO position.

He testified that while serving as a career service employee, he personally requested a reduction in his annual salary to $95,000, significantly lower than the $135,000 per year he received under his CEO contract.

The COO said assertions that he remained at the same salary level throughout the transition were inaccurate.

Gov’t shipyard CEO resignation confirmed by governor

2026-10-20

Differences with two Board members

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The resignation of American Samoa Shipyard Services Authority Chief Executive Officer Carlos Sanchez was publicly confirmed by Governor Pulaali'i Nikolao Pula during his press conference last week, bringing to a close a long tenure that saw significant changes at the government-owned shipyard.

Responding to questions from KHJ News Director Monica Miller, Governor Pulaali'i confirmed that Sanchez had submitted his resignation and that it had been accepted. The Governor said the matter would now be referred to the Shipyard Services Authority Board of Directors, which will be responsible for beginning the search for a new chief executive.

"He did hand in his resignation, and I have accepted it," Pulaali'i said. "The Board will be notified, and I want them to begin looking for a new CEO."

While acknowledging Sanchez's departure, the Governor took time to commend his contributions to the shipyard and the progress made during his years at the helm.

"I want to say this: Carlos has been a magnificent person in the service that he has provided," Pula stated. "I visited the shipyard before I became governor when it was under former CEO Bill Emmsley. Compared to what Carlos has done, it's magnificent. He's done a lot of good."

The Governor added that although Sanchez is known for his strong management style, his leadership had produced tangible results.

"I know most of us know Carlos. Sometimes they say, 'If it's not Carlos' way, it's the highway,'" Pula remarked. "But he has accomplished a lot for the shipyard."

Further details about the resignation emerged during an interview Sanchez gave on the 93KHJ Morning Show, where he said his decision was primarily the result of ongoing disagreements with two members of the Shipyard Services Authority Board.

According to Sanchez, he informed the Governor that he would remain in the position only if board members Timothy Jones and Edgar Feliciano were removed.

When that did not happen, he chose to step down.

His comments indicate that tensions between management and certain board members may have played a significant role in his decision to resign after years of leading the government-owned facility.

Sanchez has been one of the most recognizable figures in American Samoa's maritime industry for more than a decade.

He was initially appointed CEO during the second term of the Togiola-Faoa Administration and later reappointed in February 2021 by former Governor Lemanu Peleti Mauga. He continued serving in the position after Governor Pulaali'i took office.

During his tenure, Sanchez oversaw numerous operational and infrastructure improvements at the shipyard, helping expand its capabilities and its role in servicing vessels operating throughout the region.

His leadership coincided with efforts to strengthen the shipyard's financial performance and enhance its reputation as an important maritime asset for the Territory.

With Sanchez's resignation now official, attention turns to the Shipyard Services Authority Board of Directors, which will be tasked with selecting his successor.

Current board members include Krista Haleck, Lei Veavea, Sean Gregg, Solomona Joe Moala, Roman Rishi, Timothy Jones, and Edgar Feliciano.

The board has not yet announced a timetable for identifying a replacement or whether an interim CEO will be appointed while the search is underway.

Sanchez's departure marks a significant leadership transition for one of the Territory's most important government-owned enterprises, and the board's next CEO will inherit responsibility for maintaining operations and building upon the progress made during his lengthy tenure.

Final leasing notice issued for first-ever offshore mineral lease sale

2026-10-20

Source: Bureau of Ocean Energy Management

Washington, D.C. — The Marine Minerals Administration (MMA) announced yesterday the availability of a Final Leasing Notice for an Outer Continental Shelf minerals lease sale offshore American Samoa for Lease Sale PACM-1. The notice sets out the areas offered for lease, the sale schedule, lease terms and stipulations, rental and royalty rates, and information for prospective bidders.

The notice gives prospective bidders and the public a clear account of how the sale will proceed. Lease Sale PACM-1 is scheduled for November 19, 2026, and will offer two areas offshore American Samoa.

“Critical minerals are no longer just commodities; they are a vital strategic asset in global competition, essential for reaching our energy efficiency goals, strengthening our national defense, and securing domestic supply chains,” said acting MMA Director Mike Olsen.

“MMA recognizes the ocean floor surrounding American Samoa carries cultural, economic, and environmental significance, requiring that the pursuit of National Security and energy readiness is balanced with rigorous environmental stewardship. As MMA evaluates potential deep-sea resources, its priority remains guided by science, environmental review, and meaningful engagement with the people and leadership of American Samoa.”

The Final Leasing Notice, maps and supporting materials are available at boem.gov/american-samoa. The notice is scheduled to go on public display in the Federal Register on October 20, 2026, with the auction taking place on November 19, 2026.

A winning bid and securing a lease along the OCS, by itself, does not authorize immediate permission to harvest deep-sea minerals; it only authorizes preliminary activities like mapping. MMA will manage a multi-stage post-auction regulatory process before a company can begin physical exploration, testing, or full-scale commercial harvesting.

MMA is offering two lease areas for bid in Lease Sale PACM-1

The Final Leasing Notice, including maps, supporting materials, and leasing forms, are now available at www.boem.gov/american-samoa.

Governor warns cuts to 2027 healthcare budget could impact draw down of federal funds

2026-10-19

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Governor Pulaali'i Nikolao Pula has voiced concern over reductions to healthcare funding approved by the Fono in the Fiscal Year 2027 budget, warning that the cuts could significantly affect the Territory's ability to draw down federal funds and support essential medical services.

Speaking during his weekly press conference on Wednesday, the Governor addressed legislative reductions made to both the local Medicaid matching fund and the subsidy provided to the LBJ Tropical Medical Center.

Under the budget approved by the Fono, the local Medicaid match was reduced by 50 percent, from $6 million to $3 million, while the annual subsidy for LBJ Hospital was cut from $1.6 million to $1.2 million.

Governor Pulaali'i said he is particularly concerned about the reduction in Medicaid funding, noting that the local match serves as the foundation for securing much larger amounts of federal assistance.

According to the Governor, the $3 million reduction could result in the Territory forfeiting more than $9 million in federal Medicaid funding that would otherwise be available to support healthcare services for American Samoa residents.

He emphasized that Medicaid plays a critical role in funding healthcare services for low-income residents, senior citizens, people with disabilities, and individuals requiring long-term care and medical assistance.

Governor Pulaali'i said it is important for the public to fully understand the real-world impact of the budget reductions approved by the Fono, particularly those affecting healthcare funding.

"The people deserve to hear what these cuts mean to their families," the Governor said, emphasizing that the consequences extend far beyond the dollar amounts appearing in the budget.

Explaining his concern over the reduction in the Medicaid local matching fund, Pulaali'i pointed out that every local dollar appropriated for Medicaid allows the Territory to draw down about two more dollars of federal funding. As a result, cuts to the local match have a multiplier effect, reducing not only local spending but also the federal funds available to support healthcare services.

According to the Governor, federal Medicaid funds cannot be accessed unless the American Samoa Government first provides its required matching contribution.

"You don't receive the federal money unless the local share is there first," the governor explained.

For that reason, he said the Fono's decision to reduce the Territory's Medicaid matching fund from $6 million to $3 million could have consequences far greater than the $3 million reduction itself.

"So cutting $3 million from the match does not take $3 million out of healthcare," Pulaali'i explained. "It really takes about $9.3 million out of healthcare, because $6.3 million in federal money that belongs to our people is left unclaimed. Here is what that looks like for our families. Local clinics and providers may wait a little longer to be paid, and some services may be disrupted. No new providers may be brought in, and off-island referrals are at risk. In 2024, off-island referrals were suspended for lack of funds.

"Families who need specialty care that is not available here could face that again. New services that our people have been waiting for, including personal care services in homes and communities, cannot move forward. At LBJ, the $400,000 cut falls almost entirely on personnel and supplies, which is $9 out of every $10 the subsidy pays for. In addition, LBJ subsidy helps pay for the same off-island referral program. Our sickest, the ones that are struggling for care, are squeezed in from both sides."

When asked whether he was considering calling a special session of the Fono to discuss the budget cuts and their impact with legislative leaders, Governor Pulaali'i

"Perhaps I will," the Governor replied.

However, he stressed that such a decision would depend on the administration's ongoing assessment of how the budget reductions affect essential government services, particularly healthcare, as well as future discussions with Fono leadership.

According to Pulaali'i, the administration is currently reviewing the full impact of the funding cuts approved by lawmakers and evaluating whether additional legislative action may be necessary.

The Governor also reminded reporters that he had previously sought a special session of the Fono following this year's Flag Day celebrations. However, he said legislative leaders requested that any special session be postponed until after the lawmakers' recess.

Pulaali'i explained that when the Legislature reconvened, attention quickly shifted to the FY 2027 budget process.

"When the Fono came back, things happened so fast and the budget came," the Governor said. "I didn't want to shut government down."

Rather than risk delaying passage of the budget and disrupting government operations, he said he chose to exercise his constitutional line-item veto authority after the spending measure reached his desk.

"Instead, when it came to me, I line-item vetoed some of the things and sent it back to the Fono," Pulaali'i explained.

The Governor noted that he took that action on September 30 and said that since then communication with the Legislature regarding the budget and related funding concerns has been limited.

According to Pulaali'i, the only significant legislative action he has received from the Fono since that time was the bill addressing the American Samoa Government's longstanding debt to the American Samoa Government Employees Retirement Fund (ASGERF).

That measure seeks to convert the government's more than $30 million obligation to the Retirement Fund into a formal loan arrangement, with repayment assistance to be provided by the American Samoa Telecommunications Authority (ASTCA).

Local Chapter of the American Red Cross is stepping up its preparedness efforts

2026-10-16

This year's theme: "Why You? It's a Must Right Now!"

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — As the start of the South Pacific cyclone season approaches, the American Samoa Chapter of the American Red Cross is stepping up its preparedness efforts through a Volunteer Recruitment Drive. The initiative is designed to bolster the organization's emergency response team ahead of the cyclone season, which runs from November through April, and ensure sufficient manpower is available to assist the community during natural disasters and other emergencies.

The recruitment drive officially got underway yesterday with a media outreach campaign aimed at spreading the message through as many communication channels as possible. Red Cross officials met with members of the local media to encourage broad coverage of the initiative and help reach residents across the Territory.

This year's theme, "Why You? It's a Must Right Now!" emphasizes the urgent need for community involvement in disaster preparedness and emergency response. The American Samoa Chapter has set an ambitious goal of recruiting 300 new volunteers to strengthen its capacity to respond to tropical cyclones, natural disasters, and other emergencies during the upcoming season.

In an exclusive interview with Samoa News, Lipea Uta Sui, Business Operations Coordinator for the American Samoa Chapter of the American Red Cross, said this year's campaign marks the first time the organization has launched a volunteer recruitment drive with a specific numerical target.

According to Sui, the local chapter is part of the American Red Cross Pacific Islands Region, which is headquartered in Honolulu, Hawaii and oversees operations in Hawaii, American Samoa, Guam, and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands.

Sui explained that expanding American Samoa's volunteer base has been a major focus of regional leadership since 2025. The initiative aligns with the Pacific Islands Region's long-term goal of strengthening local disaster preparedness and emergency response capabilities through increased community participation.

He noted that the growing unpredictability of weather patterns across the Pacific has highlighted the need for communities to be better prepared for emergencies. Tropical cyclones, severe storms, flooding, and other natural disasters have repeatedly impacted island nations throughout the region, causing widespread damage to homes, schools, businesses, and critical infrastructure.

"We have seen firsthand how quickly weather conditions can change and how devastating the impacts can be," Sui said. "Throughout the Pacific, storms have destroyed homes, disrupted essential services, displaced families, and, in some cases, resulted in the loss of life. That's why it is so important that we build a strong network of trained volunteers who can respond when disasters strike."

Sui emphasized that volunteers are the backbone of Red Cross operations, assisting with disaster preparedness, emergency sheltering, damage assessments, relief distribution, community outreach, and recovery efforts. By increasing the number of trained volunteers, he said, the organization hopes to strengthen the Territory's ability to respond quickly and effectively when emergencies occur.

With the cyclone season set to begin in November, the chapter hopes to recruit 300 volunteers who will help ensure communities across American Samoa are better prepared to face whatever challenges the season may bring.

He explained that while American Samoa and neighboring countries south of the Equator are preparing for the start of the tropical cyclone season, the cyclone season for Guam, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), and Hawaii, which are located north of the Equator, is approaching its end. Their tropical cyclone season typically runs from May through October.

Sui noted that recent reports indicate both Guam and Hawaii have faced significant weather threats in recent weeks. Hawaii was impacted by Hurricane Lowell in September, bringing heavy rainfall, flooding, power outages, and damaging winds. Meanwhile, Guam remains under threat from Tropical Storm Champi, prompting typhoon and flood watches for parts of the Mariana Islands.

He said these events serve as a timely reminder of the importance of disaster preparedness, as communities across the Pacific continue to face the challenges posed by severe weather and tropical cyclones.

"With weather patterns becoming increasingly unpredictable and extreme weather events capable of causing widespread damage to homes, infrastructure, and even loss of life, there is absolutely no room for complacency," said American Red Cross Business Operations Coordinator, Lipea Uta Sui.

He stressed that disaster preparedness is a shared responsibility and requires the participation of people from all sectors of the community.

"It is imperative that we build a comprehensive and diverse network of volunteers representing the many ethnic communities that make up our Territory," Sui said. "Having volunteers who can communicate effectively within their own communities will help ensure that critical information is disseminated quickly and accurately before, during, and after a natural disaster."

Sui explained that the Red Cross plans to reach out to a wide range of community groups and organizations as part of its volunteer recruitment campaign. These efforts will include engagement with the various ethnic communities residing in American Samoa as well as different church denominations throughout the Territory.

The organization is also seeking the support of the Office of Samoan Affairs, which would assist in mobilizing village mayors, village police officers, aumaga or untitled men's groups, and women's committees to serve as volunteers and support disaster response efforts at the village level.

In addition, local service organizations such as the Rotary Club, Lions Club, the American Samoa Fa'afafine Association, and other community groups will be encouraged to participate. The Red Cross also hopes to recruit volunteers from schools, government departments and agencies, local businesses, military reserve units, veterans organizations, and other sectors of the community.

According to Sui, informational flyers containing a QR code have already been distributed throughout the Territory. Individuals interested in volunteering can scan the QR code or visit redcross.org/volunteer to register online.

He noted that the same website also provides access to applications for several high-demand volunteer positions that require additional training and commitment. Interested applicants can complete and submit forms detailing their personal information, qualifications, skills, and professional experience.

Among the positions currently being filled are Disaster Action Team (DAT) members, Emergency Evacuation Shelter Workers, Recovery Care Caseworkers, and Feeding and Distribution Services Associates. These volunteers play critical roles in disaster response by assisting affected families, operating emergency shelters, distributing food and relief supplies, and helping communities recover in the aftermath of emergencies.

Sui said the names of individuals who register as volunteers or apply for specialized positions will be entered into the American Red Cross Pacific Islands Region volunteer database. Applications will be reviewed and monitored by Senior Volunteer Recruitment Specialist Mary Finley, who will maintain contact with applicants regarding training opportunities, orientation sessions, and potential deployment during emergencies.

Those seeking additional information about volunteer opportunities or the recruitment campaign may contact Mary Finley via email at Mary.Finley@redcross.org.

With the tropical cyclone season set to begin next month, Red Cross officials are urging residents not to wait until a storm threat materializes before becoming involved. Instead, they are encouraging individuals to take proactive steps now to help build a stronger and more resilient community capable of responding effectively when disasters strike.

Gov. Pulaalii asks that people of Am Samoa be patient over $10.1 Mil investment

2026-10-15

Holds his only 2nd press conference since coming to office

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Governor Pulaalii Nikolao Pula is appealing to the people of American Samoa to remain patient as efforts continue to finalize the controversial $10.1 million investment funded by interest earnings from the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA).

The investment was among several topics discussed during a press conference held yesterday afternoon — only the second such media briefing since Pulaalii took office. The governor also addressed the status of ARPA-funded projects, the recently established council overseeing opioid settlement funds, reductions in Medicaid funding, ongoing anti-drug initiatives, and spending reductions made by the Fono to the Fiscal Year 2027 Special Programs budget.

While the press conference did not reveal any major developments regarding the investment itself, administration officials disclosed that legal representatives for McKinley Beech Tree (MBT) are now leading discussions with officials in the United Arab Emirates in an effort to complete the transaction.

According to the governor, the American Samoa Government's participation in the investment is expected to generate approximately $100.1 million through a series of tranche payments once the transaction is completed.

"The American Samoa Government's initial participation in the $10.1 million investment is expected to yield $100.1 million through tranche payments," Pulaalii said. "The funding is contingent upon the United Arab Emirates transmitting capital investment funds to McKinley Beech Tree in Dubai."

The governor explained that MBT Executive Director Gregory Burkholder has engaged legal counsel to facilitate communications with parties in the UAE and help move the funding process forward.

Pulaalii emphasized that the proposal is about more than a financial return.

He said the transaction could open the door to a broader relationship with MBT that may attract additional private investment into American Samoa.

"Beyond the immediate financial benefits, this transaction represents an opportunity to establish a lasting partnership with MBT," the governor said. "Such a relationship could bring additional private capital investments to American Samoa's infrastructure, economic development projects, and long-term growth."

The governor also sought to address the political controversy surrounding the investment, urging residents not to allow the issue to create divisions within the community.

"I respectfully and humbly ask the people of American Samoa for your patience and understanding as the parties work toward completing this transaction," Pulaalii said. "While differences of opinion have emerged, we should not allow this matter to divide our Territory.

"The anticipated revenues and investments represent opportunities that could benefit all of our people, not just a particular branch of government or political interest."

Governor Pulaalii then turned to his Executive Advisor for Finance, Brett Butler, to provide a more detailed update on the status of the investment.

Butler said he remains in regular communication with Gregory Burkholder and that MBT's legal team is now directly engaged with UAE officials regarding the transaction.

"As of this morning, they have taken their legal counsel to discuss with the UAE the progress of this funding opportunity," Butler said.

According to Butler, the matter is currently in the hands of UAE investors, who are conducting their own review to ensure the proposed funding arrangement satisfies their requirements.

He said the involvement of legal counsel is intended to help facilitate the process and expedite the transfer of funds.

Members of the media questioned Butler about previous timelines he had provided for the arrival of the investment proceeds, noting that the anticipated returns had not materialized on the dates previously discussed.

In response, Butler reiterated that MBT's legal representatives are actively trying to move the process forward.

He said MBT has indicated that once legal issues are resolved and approval is received, the UAE funding could be transferred into MBT's Dubai account within approximately 72 hours.

"Once they do that, they've given us three days to get that investment from the UAE into the MBT Dubai account," Butler explained. "Once they receive it, they will notify us."

From there, Butler said, the funds would require an additional two to three days to reach the American Samoa Government's account at Zions Bank, depending on processing and transfer times.

For now, however, Butler acknowledged that officials are still waiting for a definitive funding date.

"As soon as we know that date, we will announce it publicly," he said.

The issue of insurance coverage associated with the $10.1 million investment also resurfaced during the press conference.

The governor was asked about testimony presented during recent Senate Government Operations Committee hearings. During those hearings, Butler stated that the investment was protected by insurance. However, officials representing insurance companies mentioned during the hearings reportedly testified that the American Samoa Government had not directly purchased insurance coverage for the transaction.

Asked about the apparent contradiction, Governor Pulaalii defended the administration's position.

"The people who testified in that hearing were the wrong people," Pulaalii said. "They were not involved with the insurance at all, although one of them may have been affiliated with a company connected to the transaction. The Fono, I'm sorry to say, was talking to the wrong people."

Butler was again called upon to clarify how the insurance coverage was structured.

According to Butler, the insurance arrangement was not negotiated directly between ASG and the insurers.

Instead, he said MBT handled that process through an insurance broker.

"The insurance was between ASG and MBT," Butler explained. "MBT engaged an insurance broker called First Gate, which then communicated with an insurer known as Trade and Merchant."

According to Butler, Trade and Merchant subsequently retained Southern Pacific Insurance Company to act as guarantor for the transaction.

He said the administration has provided the Fono with a policy certificate documenting the arrangement.

"But regarding the engagement itself, ASG did not directly communicate with those insurance companies," Butler said. "MBT worked through its broker, which coordinated with Trade and Merchant and Southern Pacific Insurance. That was the course of the transaction."

The investment remains under scrutiny following a series of Senate hearings examining both the legality of the expenditure and the safeguards put in place to protect public funds.

A preliminary report was issued by the Senate Government Operations Standing Committee on October 8, 2026 and forwarded to the Senate President, with a more detailed final report expected to be issued before the end of October 2026. The preliminary report includes the standing committee’s recommendations for further actions to follow up with the investigation. Samoa News will report on the preliminary findings of the Senate Standing Committee and its recommendations in tomorrow’s issue.

Meanwhile, administration officials continue to express confidence that the transaction will ultimately be completed and that the anticipated returns will materialize once the funding process in the UAE is finalized.

Official opening of lawmakers new offices at the Fono complex celebrated

2026-10-13

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — After the House of Representatives and Senate concluded their final sessions of the Fourth Regular Session of the 39th Legislature last Friday, lawmakers gathered for a milestone event many had been waiting years to celebrate: the official opening of their new offices at the Fono complex in Fagatogo.

The occasion marked the end of a long period during which senators and faille operated without permanent offices following the demolition of the old Fono building in 2017. For nearly nine years, lawmakers conducted legislative business from temporary locations while construction of the new legislative complex progressed.

The opening ceremony had originally been scheduled to take place in the open-air courtyard separating the new office wing from the main Fono building. However, intermittent showers prompted organizers to move the event indoors to the building's spacious main foyer.

The ceremony was relatively intimate, attended primarily by senators, faille, legislative staff, and a handful of family members, including the wives of several lawmakers. Notably absent were representatives of the executive and judicial branches, as well as officials from Paramount Builders, the company responsible for constructing the new offices, as well as the new iconic Fono building.

The service began with an opening prayer and sermon delivered by Reverend Faalili Otineru of CCCAS Fagalii, who offered blessings for the new facility and for those who will occupy it in service to the people of American Samoa.

Following the religious service, lawmakers and guests moved to the office wing for the ceremonial portion of the program. There, the wives of Senate President Tuaolo Manaia Fruean and House Speaker Savali Talavou Ale cut celebratory cakes prepared for the occasion.

The festivities continued with a ribbon-cutting ceremony symbolizing the official opening of the offices. Two ribbons were cut, one for the western wing housing the offices of House members and another for the eastern wing occupied by senators. Mrs. Fruean and Mrs. Ale performed the honors, formally opening the facilities for use.

In addition to the new office space, visitors entering the main Fono building are now greeted by an extensive display of historical and contemporary portraits honoring legislative leaders.

Along the Senate side of the foyer, a series of black-and-white portraits chronicles the history of the upper chamber's leadership, beginning with Leiato Tunu, who served as Senate President in 1948, and continuing through successive administrations to the current Senate President, Tuaolo.

The House display features portraits of current members of the House of Representatives, with Speaker Savali Talavou Ale and Vice Speaker Fetui Fetu Jr. prominently positioned above the photographs of their colleagues.

The portrait project was completed by the American Samoa Council on Arts, Culture and Humanities, under the direction of Ammon Fepulea'i and his staff, who photographed, prepared, and mounted the images now displayed throughout the foyer.

For many lawmakers, the opening represented more than the dedication of a new office building. It marked the completion of a long-awaited chapter in the Legislature's history and the restoration of a permanent workspace where senators and representatives can meet with constituents, conduct legislative business, and carry out their duties under one roof.

For many House representatives/ faipule, the opening of the new offices was an achievement tinged with uncertainty. After waiting nearly nine years for a permanent legislative home, lawmakers finally received the office space they had long anticipated.

However, with the general election just weeks away, many of those who toured their new offices on Friday do not know whether they will return after November to occupy them. Only those faipule running unopposed can be assured of returning to the offices when the 40th Legislature convenes in January 2027.

Samoa News points out that in addition to their salaries, senators and faipule receive a $65,000 annual office expense allowance, while the Senate President and House Speaker receive $85,000 per year.

The office allowance is intended to cover expenses incurred in the discharge of official legislative duties. Under American Samoa law, legislators are not required to provide an accounting of how the allowance is spent, and they can also choose to pay taxes on the amount or not.

Not paying taxes on the office allowance has been a matter of contention with the Tax Office, who maintain that taxes are required. As it stands, it is still up to the individual lawmaker.

If they do pay taxes on the allowance, it would be included in the calculation of their retirement deductible which would then lead to a higher retirement amount received when they are no longer serving or retire from senatorial duties. Samoa News understands that very few lawmakers — both senators and faipule — have chosen to pay taxes on their office allowance.

BACKGROUND

The final cost of the total Fono Complex project continues to remain unknown, with no official accounting publicly announced.

When it began, the total was just above $10 Million for the main Fono building, and it did not contain lawmakers’ offices. However, after several setbacks that included re-building the foundation to meet federal flood zone standards, COVID time/ supply delays, and then plans added for the new office wing, the total is said to be around $38 million. It is not known, if this amount includes the cost of furniture and fixtures, parking lot, etc., with some estimating the final cost to be around $60 Million, when all is said and done.

White Sunday is centerpiece of 3-day holiday weekend

2026-10-09

By

Samoa News staff

reporters@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — It will be a busy weekend in American Samoa as residents gear up for White Sunday, the centerpiece of a 3-day holiday that ends with Columbus Day, also known as Indigenous Peoples Day, on Monday.

WHITE SUNDAY

Introduced in the islands by Christian missionaries in the 1800s, White Sunday has become a special holiday, with children treated to the best — from White Sunday outfits to food served during family toanai. It is always celebrated on the second Sunday of October and children are treated as kings and queens for their day.

Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata released the following statement for White Sunday:

“Together as a people, we look forward to this special Sunday featuring the children of our islands, knowing they are a gift and heritage to us directly from the Lord (Psalm 127:3). This happy occasion also serves as a reminder to hold to our faith throughout every age of life

“Although my role as a Congresswoman fills most of my time day to day, my roles as a Christian, and as a mother and grandmother will always be even more important. These are God-given roles and blessings. I will be enjoying the wonderful children of our islands on White Sunday through the eyes and heart of a mother and grandmother.

“We thank God for the children of our islands, their bright futures, and God’s good plan for their lives. On this White Sunday, we entrust our youth to our Heavenly Father’s blessing, knowing that ‘the Lord takes pleasure in his people’ (Psalm 149:4). Have a joyful White Sunday!”

White Sunday is also celebrated in other parts of the world where Samoan communities are located, such as Honolulu, Los Angeles, San Francisco, and New Zealand.

As usual, police are beefing up road patrols today and tomorrow because of the expected traffic, and are calling on drivers to watch out for pedestrians, especially young children.

Local stores, bakeries and other merchants are preparing for White Sunday shopping with clothes, food and beverages. Lots of ice cream, in a variety of flavors is available in stores, as well as cakes and pies from local bakeries.

Samoa News staff and management wish all the children of the world a day, such as our White Sunday, filled with special moments of loving-kindness, celebrating our children as gifts of God.

COLUMBUS DAY/ INDIGENOUS PEOPLE’S DAY

Governor Pulaali'i Nikolao Pula has declared this coming Monday, Oct 12, 2026 as a government holiday in American Samoa — Columbus/ indigenous People’s Day — where all government offices will be closed, including the territorial bank.

As per usual for federal holidays, only essential employees will be required to perform services on that day and will receive holiday wages in accordance with applicable laws and regulations.

The governor urged in his general memorandum, “Please take this opportunity to rest and spend meaningful time with family and loved ones. Have a safe and enjoyable holiday weekend.”  He also thanked government employees for their continued service and dedication to the people of American Samoa.

Indigenous People’s Day has been federally recognized as a federal holiday along with Columbus Day — beginning in 2020 — with the Biden Administration proclaiming the second Monday in October a “day in honor of our diverse history and the Indigenous peoples who contribute to shaping this Nation.”

The US post office and all federal and ASG offices will be closed on Monday, with most businesses celebrating the day also — with grocery stores and gas stations usually the only businesses staying open on that day. Samoa News will not publish on Monday and the office will be closed so staff can enjoy the long holiday weekend with their families.

Have a safe and happy 3-day weekend American Samoa!
